_about: What VibeLearn can check, for people and agents (an orchestrator's describe_capabilities). Each check: what it proves, its lanes, scope (system: works on any game that keeps docs/TEST-CONTRACT.md; game: written for one game; mixed: system probes plus game segments), cost, what it needs, and which changed files call for it (tools/affected.mjs). Reports: tools/lib/report.mjs; the gate: tools/quality.mjs.

learning.asks: Is the learning real? Every puzzle solvable without a wrong answer, no softlocks, real decisions, nothing skippable, first tries honest, checkpoints earned.

flow.asks: Can the game be played start to end in every input mode, through every handoff, without getting stuck?

world.asks: Can every goal be reached on foot, is each action offered where the goal points, does the player stay on the map?

pacing.asks: How long is the fastest legal run, per checkpoint? (tracked: a stop that gets much shorter may have lost its learning)

timing.asks: Do lines and cutscenes leave no overlaps (a line cut off by its own speaker) and no dead air?

robustness.asks: Does it survive mashing, reloading, pausing, skipping, rotating, random play, edited saves?

performance.asks: Does it hold frame rate on the low-end phone at the chosen resolution? Are assets within budget?
performance.judged_by: tools + the frame-rate test on the device

sound.asks: Is the mix right: voices clear, ambience and music under them, nothing clipping?

content.asks: Is the story and station data valid and in house style (short sentences, no broken jumps, content agrees with its rules)?

system.asks: Is the game kept apart from the system (kit and system tools name nothing from the game), is its manifest valid, do the checkers catch what they should (self-tests)?

comprehension.asks: Blind: does a newcomer who was told nothing understand what the game means to show, and how did it come out (unprompted, when asked about their own words, only when pointed at a moment, only after being told)? Would they play the next part?
comprehension.judged_by: blind AI play-testers and an interviewer (playserver), then people

feel.asks: Does it look, move, sound and feel right on a real device: camera comfort, animation, art, music, control feel, humour landing?
feel.judged_by: a person on a real device (Desmic: Galaxy F15 and laptop). No tool can pass this lane.

checks.proves: Every story script, station list, rules spec, progress spec and the manifest is valid; content agrees with its rules.
Every puzzle is solvable, winnable without a wrong answer, free of softlocks, and every declared decision has right and wrong answers. Prints the answer keys.
The system's data checks (manifest, story, stations, progress, rules proofs, intent) work on a second, deliberately different game (fixtures/night-market): they are not one game's.
Pure kit rules hold on made-up cases: targeting (aimed beats near, priority when lined up, reach) and earned progress.
Every place that asks the player to say a thing into existence (kit/utter.ts) is solvable from the words it offers, has more than one working phrasing and at least two different ways to be wrong.

Every place in a next-word lab (kit/ngram.ts) is solvable from what the player can read by then, in any reading order; a place's lesson can't be skipped (without its key reading, nothing the engine will say works); and there is more than one wrong thing to say.
The utterance test area plays: wrong phrases fail visibly, right ones make things that work (a bridge can be walked across, a lantern lights the doorway).

The next-word lab plays: the engine suggests what it has read after a word; a word read too rarely is shown but not said; reading the builders' song lifts 'long bridge' to the top; 'let it finish' says the engine's favourite; working things can be walked across and the doorway lights.
The kit imports nothing from the game; system code names nothing from the game's world; every tool declares its scope here.
Every shipped model is within its folder's budget (triangles, draw calls, materials, bytes).
The browser's rules interpreter and the server's agree on every spec (random walks, broken specs).
The scripted journey, start to the end, as a phone (taps, thumb stick) and as a laptop (keys); contact sheet of every step.
The fastest legal run on foot: every station played from its rules alone, no learning skipped, checkpoints earned, every goal reachable, pacing per checkpoint.
Edges, walls, mashing, order, reload-scumming, pause, skip, rotate, edited saves (from the progress spec) and random play break no promise.
Cutscene lines in game time with their voiced lengths: no line cut off by its own speaker; dead air flagged.
Measured at the master bus: ambience 12–25 dB under the voices, music under them but heard, nothing clipping.
Runs the play checks one after another (never two games at once) and writes index.html with every contact sheet, pacing and timing.

checks.run: node tools/playserver.mjs --input touch --persona commuter|explorer|rarely [--intent utter --start '&lab=utter'] (blind: a tester agent gets only GET /brief, plays, stops; an interviewer agent gets GET /interview/brief; see tools/AI-PLAYTEST.md)
needs: two agents that can see screenshots
checks.proves: Blind: what a newcomer who was told nothing understood, graded by how it came out in the interview (unprompted, probed, only when pointed at, only after the reveal). Directed (--protocol directed): a tester told what to try (a loophole hunter); its findings are robustness and learning evidence, not comprehension. An AI player approximates a person; it does not replace one.

Blind play-tests side by side: how each intent item came out per run (unprompted … missed), keep-playing score, steps. For A/B variants or trends across builds; one run per variant is a lead, not a verdict.
The play-tester's brief and personas carry no word from any game's design and nothing that primes a judgement; the interview leak guard refuses design words and leading words on made-up cases.
A person's verdict on this exact build. The final word on feel; overrides nothing else (a failing check still fails).

checks.run: open the game with #bench=1 (or Pause → Run frame-rate test) on the device
checks.proves: Frame rate per quality tier and the resolution sweep, on the device itself (kit/bench.ts).
Walking under a thumb, measured: a sidestep holds its line and doesn't turn the camera, pushing along an edge slides along it, and the camera never sits inside the player's head with the body drawn.
Walks the opening routes with the real follow camera and scores each half second (player on screen, view blocked).
Replays an AI play-test's actions to reproduce a reported moment.
Prints what the game means to communicate, from its data (for the comparison step of an AI play-test).
Per-lane verdict for this build from every report: pass, fail or unresolved; never averaged.
Which checks a change calls for.
Lists every line to voice (story lines from the manifest; lines still written in this game's code by pattern).
Acts new lines with TTS (never prints or commits the key).
Writes every rules spec as JSON for the server.
Screenshots of the cutscenes every ~0.8 s of game time, for look-dev.
Serves the build, drives it as a phone or a laptop, plans paths, writes reports.
Packs the build for the claude.ai artifact.
Rewrites compiled imports for plain ES modules.
Checks the baked animation clips on the protagonist's rig.
Retargets the CC0 animation library onto the protagonist's rig, offline.
